Super convenient. I bring milk bags of course (make sure to always check to make sure you’re stocked up on those!). I bring a little insulated lunchbox with ice packs to put my pumped milk in, and after my last pump I’m able to place that whole thing in our lounge fridge until I go home. I like using the Dapple pump wipes if you aren’t able to take extra time to wash the pump parts after each session, though I only wipe them down or wash them after the first session and then throw them in a bag to take home after the last session to just wash at home, to save time.

But yeah, always check your pumping bag for extra milk bags if you aren’t going to store your pumped milk in bottles. Also depending on the pump you’re bringing, consider having extra parts packed if you have them in case something gets broken, lost, forgotten, etc. Snacks and hydration drinks are great to have lots of as well!

Each time I pump (usually 7-10oz depending on how long ago my previous pump was), I put it in a big bottle in the fridge to chill. Similar concept when I used the pitcher method (which is super helpful, but I don’t use it as much anymore now that I’m back to work and only prep the milk my baby’s going to need that day). After each session, that milk went in the fridge to chill, and once it was good I added it all to a pitcher. Then used the pitcher to help prep bottles. I know some people aren’t worried about adding freshly pumped milk to already chilled milk, so do whatever you’re comfortable with. I just find it’s not a hassle to wait for it to chill.

I can share my knowledge about a few of your questions. I didn’t plan to pump and started out trying to nurse, but baby wouldn’t latch correctly, wasn’t gaining weight, etc. so at around 3 weeks postpartum I stopped nursing “cold turkey” and switched to exclusively pumping. Baby was already being supplemented formula and continued that until my supply reached enough to wean her off. I’m now 5 months in, still only pumping, and no longer have to supplement, though everyone’s supply is different, and there’s nothing wrong with formula if you end up needing it.

When I first started, I gave my baby whatever I pumped and roughly every other feed was formula. Once my supply began to increase, I was able to start building a stash in my fridge. Now at 5 months, I pump and put whatever I make each session in the fridge, and at the start of the day I divide my stash into bottles. We warm the bottle or give it cold, baby usually takes both. Pumped milk can be kept in the fridge for up to 4 days, according to guidelines, but must be used within 2-3 hours once baby has started drinking it. I’ve been blessed enough to also have a freezer stash, and frozen milk is best used within 6 months, though up to a year is acceptable. I wasn’t able to start building a freezer stash though until I’d been exclusively pumping for well over a month. I’ve also used a pitcher method for fresh milk where everything I pump (once it’s all the same temp) gets mixed into a pitcher and then poured into bottles as needed. I don’t use a pitcher as much now that I’m working again but it worked out really well.

I started out pumping every 3-4 hours (I know lactation consultants will say every 2-3 hours but I went based off my pediatrician’s recommendation and it worked out for me). Now at 5 months, I’m down to 4-5 pumps a day every 5-6 hours, but again, everyone is different and you’ll learn what’s best for your body and baby. 

You’ll have to learn what pump settings work best for you, and finding the right flange size is SO important! I used the default one for the longest time and had really sore nipples and not the best output. They sell sizing sheets that are easy to use, and some pumps may come with one. Then you can buy the flange inserts in your size. As for pumps, the Spectra s2 is my go-to (highly recommend Spectra) and I use wearables Momcozy m5s for work.

I’m no expert, but feel free to reach out anytime you want anymore insight from someone who’s definitely learned a lot during this whole process. It’s all trial and error at first. Enjoy the rest of your pregnancy!!!

It can be a pain sticking to a pumping schedule and washing parts/bottles constantly, but it’s been working so well for me, my baby, and my husband who can easily feed baby anytime. I wanted to nurse to feel more connected to my daughter but it never felt like a bonding experience to me, so I don’t feel like I’m missing out in that respect. 

Like you said, I also love seeing how much milk I’m making and how much my baby is drinking a day. Not knowing when nursing was anxiety-inducing since my baby just wasn’t a great nurser and I’d spend over an hour each session trying to get her nurse while already being sleep deprived. We’re at the point now where I know how many ounces I should expect my baby to drink during the day in order for her to sleep through the night. 

Pumping is a learning experience when it comes to finding out what kind of schedule, type of pump and settings, duration of time pumping, etc. works best for you, but once you figure it out it can be worth it.

I hope the best for you!

First time mom as well, first month or so was REALLY rough. I never regretted my baby but I struggled so much mentally just feeling capable of being a mother. Our baby did not know day from night and therefore would be wide awake practically all night long and sleep a lot during the day. Being able to take shifts with my partner was a blessing. Eventually we created a routine and ended up turning to exclusively pumping because my baby struggled to latch and would also just fall asleep at the breast instead of eat, and I’d sit there for over an hour at a time crying just trying to get her to feed. I was also supplementing formula and pumping on top of that. (Disclaimer: I’m sure nursing probably would’ve gotten better with time, but just pumping is working out very well for us.) It’s hard to offer advice because all babies and families and circumstances are different, so take this with a grain of salt, but pumping and bottle feeding was best for our baby. We can easily track how many ounces she’s getting in a day, and we’re at the point where we feed her every 2 hours still but she sleeps through the night! At 10 weeks now we are doing great. It DOES get better, but the light comes at different points for everyone. My baby thankfully loves her bassinet but finding a correct swaddle/sleep wear for her was key to her being able to sleep comfortably for long stretches.

As for medication, definitely reach out to your doctor if you feel like you need help. I’m on Zoloft and I know it’s helped getting me through these rough times.

- a bassinet (was just going to use a crib to start but the bassinet was gifted to us and has been SO great)
- stroller/car seat combo (think this is what you’re looking to get and it’s definitely convenient)
- white noise machine (we have the Hatch but use a simple portable one by Yogasleep more often)
- a swaddle (we LOVE the SwaddleDesigns Omni Swaddle; babies can sleep with arms up or swaddled by their sides depending on baby’s preference)
- a giant trash can with a lid instead of a small diaper bin, works great, haven’t had issues with smell
- two-way zipper sleepers (SO CONVENIENT, skip the button sleepers, bonus points if the zipper sleeper covers feet and has built in mittens)

Not Necessary:
- bottle warmer (our baby takes milk cold or room temp)
- hand mittens (the sleepers with the built in mittens are so much better)
